This was my Diablo when I couldn't afford to play Diablo, and it could even run on my old PC, which would start heating up if I opened too many Chrome tabs.
What hooked me was the skill tree, the spell combinations, and the global chat, which was always funny and chill (apart from the occasional bot spam).
It's also quite impressive how the developers keep pumping out quality content and new mechanics every season, giving players new things to interact with without making older content obsolete. The devs are also pretty smart when it comes to planning their expansions so they don't overlap with PoE 2. This way, you'll have a steady supply of PoE crack all year round.

My main issue is having to replay the whole damn campaign for what feels like the 50th time. But I also understand why they do it: it forces you to become more familiar with your build, experiment with different setups, and maybe even come up with something innovative.

I highly recommend this game, especially if you already have experience with this genre of games

This is the greatest game ever made. Insane levels of depth and is really rewarding for hardcode players. There is incredible diversity in how people approach builds. poe.ninja's ladder indexes thousands of people. Every league you can find someone high up on the ladder who is using a trash skill and finding the 3 or 4 mechanics they can combine to make it worthwhile. One thing I saw this league was lightning warp + max duration in order to run heist efficiently.

Very pro-player developers. Leagues are every 3 months and provide tons of new content, balance updates, and a fresh economy. After those 3 months, your characters and items are sent to "standard league" which is the permanent league where tons of legacy versions of items are floating around. It's an amazing way to keep things fresh and I've never quite seen a game that operates around a set schedule like this. Every new league launch PoE hits top player numbers on Steam and gets a wave of hype.

The only thing that's not great about PoE is the new player experience. As a new player you are going to have absolutely no idea what you are doing, and your build is going to suck. You'll probably have to restart in order to get a build that can finish the campaign. And most experienced PoE players consider the campaign to be like "the tutorial". Mapping is where the real game starts and opens up all of the endgame strategies and content.

One of the best games ever made—if you can survive the learning cliff (700+ Hours In)

I have put over 700 hours into Path of Exile, and I am telling you straight: this is easily one of the best games I have ever played. 

Even so, my stats are kind of embarrassing—across all these seasons, I've only actually made it to the maps twice. The game is brutal! When I first started, I couldn't get past level 50 or reach Act 6 without constantly dying. I would rage quit, uninstall, leave the game for months, and then inevitably come back when a new league dropped to try again. 

And that is the beauty of PoE. Every single time I came back, I learned something new, got a bit better, and pushed a little further. The sheer depth and content of this game never get old. The build variety and complexity are unmatched, and no matter how many times it kicks my teeth in, I will always come back to check out a new league. 

Verdict: It's punishing, it has a legendary learning curve, and it will humble you—but it is an absolute masterpiece of an ARPG. Highly recommended if you love deep, endlessly rewarding progression.

Pros:
* The core gameplay is great. You kill huge hordes of monsters.
* The skill gem system is cool. You can build your own skill.
* Mapping is arguably the best end game system in gaming.
* It's free! If you like it, you will want to spend like $30 on stash tab for quality-of-life.
* Great graphics, controls and production quality.
* Tons of fun content.
* Intricate and cool build options.
* The trade system is arguably the best in gaming.

Cons:
* Too many one-shot mechanics.
* The boss design is often very poor. You must learn the boss mechanics by heart, and the game doesn't teach you those mechanics.
* It is extremely imbalanced. It's not "anything goes". There are only a few "good" builds.
* Off-screening.
* There is grinding.
* Maps have become bloated with content you don't want to interact with.
* Playing standard is miserable because your build often gets nerfed and becomes obsolete. You must play league, which means you must constantly start over. Some people enjoy that. I don't enjoy it because it takes many hours (estimately at least 40) to get a character to the endgame.
* The campaign is not enjoyable. It's boring.
* There is no multiplayer. It is a single player game where you can trade with other players who also play single player.
* Melee builds are much worse than ranged. The clear speed is too low.
* Every monster in the game has stun on hit.
* In spite of much cool content, the addition of the "atlas tree" made it meaningless to interact with most of the content because it became too unrewarding.

I almost only played standard (the permanent league where you never start over). I got tired of the nerfs. The final straw for me was when they changed the rules for socket colors. Players in standard had perfect items with 6 white sockets, which required tons of investment. Then the developers suddenly reversed it and said that white sockets are now strictly worse. It felt like an insult. All my items became worse and I can't fix them because they are mirrored.

I recommend the game for its good parts, but you must play league, not standard. For most players, playing league is probably a too big time investment.

I came in as someone who's been only a "casual" ARPG player. I'm a woman in my 40s, and I've been gaming ever since I got the NES I begged for Christmas in 1990. When I was in my 30s, literally 90% of my gaming focused on JRPGs. But in the past few years, I've reduced JRPGs to about 10-15% of my "gaming diet," with a lot more genre variety, including games that aren't RPGs at all.

I probably played OG Diablo and Diablo II a bit as a teenager. Earlier this year, I sunk some hours into Grim Dawn, tried some other ARPGs, and I've now got an original EXE of Diablo II: Lord of Destruction running in Wine outside of Steam, on my Linux desktop. 

I know n00bs are usally scared away from PoE due to the immense skill... not a tree, more like a series of skill forests. I followed some of the advice from PoE YouTubers, I got a loot filter right away and I started following a build guide for a melee attack optimized Scion. But after allocating several points, I realized that the build guide didn't quite align with the skill "forest" I had. I did spend the first several points on upgrading my strength. And now at level 32, I have a few nice attack traits, such as impale anf bleed.

Now that I'm navigating the skill "forest" with a lot more confidence, seeing patterns in how it's laid out while following the general advice to specialize rather than try to make my Scion a "Jill of all trades."

I'm having a lot of fun. I'm glad the Trials of Ascendancy aren't complicated puzzles, The puzzles in CrossCode were bad enough, I don't want them in my more Diablo like ARPGs. 

I'm still not sure how to be more active in my league other than to check the events board (empty for now), and play those sea maps for Valerie. When I know other players can see my character, I will likely buy a few cosmetics.

It took some fiddling to get the game to run well even though this is a mid tier gaming laptop from 2021. It's almost certainly because I'm running a version of Gentoo Linux, something I do because I'm a cybersecurity specialist and anti Gen AI political activist. 

If you have any sort of Linux distro, I strongly recommend going to ProtonDB before you launch the game for the first time and choose the version of Proton, and best launcher settings for your distro. Then, while in the game settings, switch networking (under the game tab) to either auto or predictive, never lockstep. I think I found predictive to be best. Even though my network connectivity is steady and fast, lockstep tends to lock me on the loading screen.

Once I had the right version of Proton and launcher settings (including "no logo"?), and tweaked the in-game settings a bit, with my loot filter from filterblade dot xyz manually added (adding from the filterblade web app didn't work for me, search DuckDuckGo for "Path of Exile Linux loot filter location" if you need to know where to put it in your Linux PC's file system), the game has been running great, with loading screens not lasting more than a couple of seconds and always 60 FPS or more. 

I really appreciate how Chris Wilson and the rest of GGG appear to be very pro-consumer and have no interest in Gen AI or any of that horrifying crap. 

To n00bs, don't be afraid of the skill "forest." Zoom in and out of it, and make note of the patterns of skills in it. Also keep in mind that the kind of attack or magic skills that would consume MP in a JRPG usually come from gems. Make sure to put gems in your equipment ASAP! And keep most  of the same gems through the campaign and end game, because they get more powerful and level up as you use them more.

Path of Exile is an outstanding free-to-play action RPG that delivers an incredibly deep and demanding adventure through a world consumed by darkness, corruption, and supernatural horrors. Developed and published by Grinding Gear Games, it distinguishes itself through extraordinary character customization, challenging combat, and an enormous collection of interconnected progression systems. Set on the hostile continent of Wraeclast, the game places players in the role of an exile fighting to survive against terrifying creatures and powerful adversaries. Its greatest achievement is the freedom it provides to experiment with different playstyles, although that same complexity can make the experience intimidating for newcomers. For players who appreciate intricate mechanics and long-term character development, it offers one of the most substantial experiences available in the genre.

The atmosphere immediately establishes a grim and unforgiving identity. Abandoned settlements, corrupted wildernesses, ancient ruins, and grotesque monsters create a convincing world where danger feels ever-present. The narrative gradually reveals the disturbing history of Wraeclast through quests, dialogue, environmental storytelling, and encounters with memorable characters. Although the lore is extensive and fascinating, its presentation sometimes takes a secondary role to relentless combat and equipment progression. Nevertheless, the dark fantasy setting remains compelling, supported by excellent environmental design, unsettling sound effects, and atmospheric music that reinforces the feeling of exploring a civilization devastated by supernatural forces.

Combat is fast, destructive, and remarkably flexible. Players can specialize in melee attacks, ranged weapons, elemental spells, summoned allies, traps, and numerous unconventional combinations. Defeating large groups of enemies with carefully developed abilities creates an immensely satisfying sense of power, while challenging bosses demand awareness, preparation, and appropriate defensive strategies. The skill gem system is particularly impressive because abilities can be modified through support gems, allowing seemingly ordinary attacks to evolve into devastating combinations. However, encounters can become visually chaotic when numerous projectiles and effects overwhelm the screen. Certain character builds also encourage repetitive ability usage, making extended grinding sessions occasionally monotonous.

Character progression represents the game's most distinctive accomplishment. Its enormous passive skill tree provides an astonishing degree of freedom, allowing players to construct highly specialized characters without being completely restricted by traditional class identities. Ascendancy specializations introduce additional layers of customization, while equipment modifiers and skill interactions create countless opportunities for experimentation. Discovering effective combinations can be incredibly rewarding, especially when a carefully planned build begins overcoming previously impossible challenges. Unfortunately, the learning curve is exceptionally steep. Newcomers may struggle to understand complicated mechanics, and poorly distributed passive points can significantly weaken a character. The game rewards research and patience but offers comparatively little forgiveness for inexperienced decisions.

Equipment acquisition and crafting provide another compelling foundation for progression. Defeated enemies frequently drop weapons, armor, accessories, and valuable crafting materials, encouraging constant experimentation with different combinations of attributes. The unconventional currency system gives numerous resources practical crafting functions, creating a fascinating relationship between item improvement and trading. Finding a rare piece of equipment or successfully crafting a powerful upgrade can feel genuinely exciting. However, randomized outcomes occasionally make progression frustrating, particularly when substantial resources disappear without producing worthwhile improvements. Inventory management also becomes increasingly demanding as players accumulate enormous quantities of equipment and specialized materials.

The endgame offers exceptional longevity through the Atlas of Worlds, challenging maps, formidable bosses, and numerous specialized activities. Completing the main campaign opens the door to increasingly sophisticated progression systems that encourage players to refine their characters and pursue more difficult encounters. Challenge leagues further enhance replayability by introducing fresh mechanics and opportunities to begin new adventures. These features make the game particularly appealing to dedicated players who enjoy optimization and continuous improvement. However, the sheer amount of available content can feel overwhelming, and reaching the highest levels of progression often requires considerable grinding and detailed mechanical knowledge.

Multiplayer adds another dimension through cooperative encounters, trading, and community interaction. Players can collaborate against dangerous enemies or participate in an extensive economy where valuable equipment and crafting resources are exchanged. The game also supports independent progression, although a persistent internet connection remains necessary. Its free-to-play model is commendable because the core adventure and substantial endgame content are accessible without mandatory purchases. Most optional transactions involve cosmetics, while additional stash tabs provide meaningful storage convenience. These purchases are not required to enjoy the campaign, but dedicated players may find them increasingly useful.

From a technical perspective, the game delivers impressive environmental detail, distinctive monster designs, and spectacular combat effects. Its visual presentation successfully captures the brutality of its setting, although performance can fluctuate during encounters involving numerous enemies and elaborate abilities. Steam Deck compatibility is officially rated Playable, meaning the game can be enjoyed on Valve's handheld system but is not fully Verified. Controller support makes combat accessible, although navigating complicated menus, managing inventory, and examining detailed equipment descriptions can feel cumbersome on the smaller display. Graphically demanding encounters may also require reduced settings for smoother performance.

Ultimately, Path of Exile is a remarkable achievement in action RPG design, offering exceptional customization, rewarding combat, and almost overwhelming replayability. Its greatest weaknesses are its intimidating complexity, occasional performance problems, demanding inventory management, and reliance on repetitive grinding. Nevertheless, these shortcomings rarely diminish the satisfaction of mastering its elaborate systems and developing increasingly powerful characters. It is particularly recommended for players who enjoy strategic character building, challenging encounters, and extensive endgame progression. Those seeking a casual adventure may find its demands exhausting, but dedicated enthusiasts will discover an extraordinarily rewarding experience.

[H1]So what's it about?[/H1]
In POE you are a criminal sentenced to death but instead shipped to the cursed continent of Wraeclast. You start with nothing and end up fighting Gods and other divine being. But to get there you will go through many beautifully crafted levels with many systems. At first it is intimidating and for your first run I highly recommend using a guide from for example [url=https://mobalytics.gg/poe/builds] Mobalytics [/url].

POE is an older game but can be measured against new releases as it has received and continues to receive updated. I've been an avid fan of Diablo and Diablo 2 since they were released (I was one of the first in D2 in Europe to hit lvl 99 back in the day). D3 was OK but not what I was looking into an ARPG and I've avoided D4 ever since the "don't you have phones" and all of the monetization; it's clear the Blizzard of old is no longer there.

POE is F2P but it doesn't mean P2W. Every couple of months new supporter packs are released that are time limited. But they are just cosmetics and the game comes with plenty. Only buy those if you want to support the developers. At most you probably spend about £30 to make your life easier with more inventory tabs but only gets those after you've played the game for a while and it's still not required for the first play through but it will help a lot managing all the loot you collect later on. Consider the campaign the trial or demo version to see if the game is for you.

You pick one of the available 7 classes when you start the game. As you progress you can then further specialise the class in the direction you like. There is so much to choose from that it will keep you busy for a long time. 

The campaign has 10 acts and those are really just the tutorial to avoid overloading you with the many systems POE has. After that the real game begins and it's all about completing maps at an increased difficulty for better rewards. Following that you arrive at the real end-game. It's a big game for sure :-).

It's great solo but multiplayer is good too. There is even PVP if you're interested in that. 

[H1]The good[/H1]
It has the most extensive systems I have ever seen in any ARPG. Just the skill tree alone is massive. This allows for a lot of experimentation to find the ideal setup. Your class is just a starting point and you can adjust how you feel fit.

I love the voice acting, the enemies and the graphical effects; GGG voice actors and artists are some of the best in class. 

There are many different leagues you can play (comparable to seasons in other games), including hard core and you can build even your own if you feel like.

The developers play their game and there are frequent updates. Tournaments are organised and if you watch them on Twitch you even get nice stuff from time to time.

The inner loot goblin is always satisfied when doing one of the many side activities in game. There is so much to collect and there is a variation of activities to keep it all fresh. 

You have your own hideout that you can decorate as you please. Later this becomes your central hub.

There is in-game trading with other players and multiplayer is supported. There is also a [url= https://www.pathofexile.com/trade ]trade post [/url] where you can buy and sell items you want or find.
The game plays really fast at times - much higher speed than D2; which is great it’s a constant adrenaline rush. The drawback is if your build has a weakness there is little room for error on the high end levels as it leaves you with little time to counter act.

[H1]The not so good[/H1]
There is definitely a deep learning curve hence I advise using a guide for the first play through so you get an understanding of the basics. 

End game (lvl 90 - 100) can be really challenging depending on your build. Some require expensive (as in rare items they are player trade) to be effective and the AI will relentlessly punish you if you have a weak build to the point you want to give up. 

To counter this you probably want to start with a character that is less depended on gear and more on skills which are easier to come by. A second build could be one that is more depending on gear as you can use the first character to farm where necessary. In general: ranged class / skills are easier than melee especially later in the game.

For every new character you create you need to go through all 10 acts of the campaign; thankfully because of the stash, your hideout and all the other different game modes, including the progress in the second part (Atlas) is account wide it's not a major issue but it would be better if you would be given the option to skip the whole campaign after the first time that you've completed it (similar to like GW2 for example).

I disapprove of the lootbox mechanic introduced every season. It's not required, it's not in your face but it can cause serious issues for people that are vulnerable to gambling addiction. The positive maybe is that all the loot from the loot boxes are released later in the MTX store but still it should not be in the game.

[H1]The DLCs[/H1]
There are no DLCs other than supporter packs that only add cosmetics to the game. There is a microtransactions (MTX) store to buy cosmetics and QoL items. If you want to get any of those wishlist them and wait for a sale (every couple of weeks). Note that some of the MTX from POE is compatible with POE2 in particular most of the inventory tabs. 

[H1]Summary[/H1]
The best time to plant a tree was 20 years ago, the second best time is now. This is true for POE. I wish I had discovered it earlier but I'm happy I did eventually. If you're into ARPG it's one of the best games to get. Highly recommended.

5000小时，n个赛季40挑战全通，n个10镜+角色的体验：糟糕至极。

(1）游戏纯纯为了不让玩家无敌通关设计，只管难，不管平衡，完全毁灭了角色扮演的本质：构筑一个角色从0开始慢慢变无敌。
用暗黑2举例，你无论选任何角色，只要靠肝都可以变得无敌通关，也都能打uber。poe恰恰相反，你无论选任何角色，哪怕用最op的bd，他也保证你有内容打不过:
自伤bd禁疗内容(emzebeler罪魂瓦尔多，uber maven 85贤主)一秒自杀打不了
瓦尔多2m远程没法打
瓦尔多罪魂百亢一击线低于150k物理300k元素没法打
瓦尔多罪魂百亢脱装-环效dps少于10亿根本不掉血
t16.5/t17 100deli多词条混沌伤(-30抗性/as extra chaos/wither)血流派都没法打即使3万血
深矿ehp低于500k没法打，dps低于1e没法打
综合一下要全通的角色需要10亿dps，走es ci，ehp500k+，元素一击300k+这样的角色赛季根本不存在。而这要求仅仅是能打，即是6门有比较大概率能过，不代表不死，甚至不代表6门一定通。
更别提终局平衡跟狗屎一样，你要强力的bd只能在以下选：t0 18耐力球ci勇士，护甲人，影陨卫士，t1 千力勇士，佣兵。这里面4/5近战，而且一共就这几个选项其他都是垃圾。你选了其他这游戏会变得奇难无比，你只能这也不打那也不打发挥阿q精神觉得自己很强。
arpg最重要的是rpg角色扮演，你今天游戏平衡狗屎一样的逼人只能玩某些他不喜欢的bd角色扮演在哪里？我是正好是近战爱好者，可是如果有个玩家他只喜欢玩弓手呢？他必须接受死的跟傻逼一样？稍微难一点的图就6门死光？

(2)装备太稀有，导致极大不公平
装备越稀有，价值越高，高到一定程度任何玩家通过努力肝都无法获得只能靠欧或者rmt导致游戏极度不公平。比如3.28赛季的双神龛腰带(加速/抗性，回响/抗性这些都是10镜起)，你要吗自己欧出来要吗rmt。人家欧一下10个镜子顶你核心玩家一赛季收益，普通玩家10赛季收益，这还怎么玩？你整个赛季肝几百小时就买人家欧一下。
装备稀有的另外一个副作用就是加剧通货膨胀的影响，1技能voices赛季初200d赛季中500d，赛季后1mirror，赛季末直接2mirror。然后你想要就要2mirror去买，这游戏稀有装备target farm都是亏损的(1voices刷simulacrum 333小时期望出一个，收益每小时对比普通策略亏损10d，即期望刷出时亏损2.3mirror)。这种稀缺加剧了通货膨胀导致的同工不同酬的不公平，赛季初肝10小时顶赛季末100小时。

(3)经济系统一坨屎，通货膨胀导致同工不同酬极度不公
这游戏核心玩家的收益从来不是刷图掉宝，从来都是靠首发优势快速积累第一桶金然后投资保值装备欺负萌新不懂赚钱。我每个赛季10镜子资本最多3镜子是自己刷的loot，起码7个镜子是靠前期200d买后期1镜的东西赚的。后进游戏的或者有工作不能全职玩的人只能看着200d的装备涨到1镜，然后他还没攒够钱买。
这游戏通货膨胀但是收益不膨胀，从第2周开始核心玩家就收益封顶了(20d/hr，有时候经济波动某些策略能30d/hr)。越到后面越没意思，你刷100个小时只为了买领先玩家开服刷1小时通货抢下来的萌新欧出来的稀缺装备。

ggg为了在一个没有足够内容的游戏里强行拖延玩家时间，现在就是纯纯的恶心人。现代游戏都这样，产能不够多做内容就调整一下现有内容的数值，加几个难度，也不管平衡，最后本来无限组合无限bd的游戏变成只有5个bd能玩。然后给你搞点永远刷不出来做不出来的装备拖延你游戏时间。最后你费尽千辛万苦做出来一身镜子装备选了最op的bd任然没法全通。他们已经不管你玩家是否在游戏中获得快乐了，他们只管赚钱。
游戏设计师脑子是有问题。各种技能卡手，boss无敌机制同时还能对玩家造成伤害，傻逼设计，烂透了。
